title: Mapping the Dark: Retrochiasmal & Chiasmal Visual Field Defects
summary: A comprehensive neuro-ophthalmic guide to localizing lesions posterior to the optic tract, featuring the nuances of congruity, macular sparing, and the differential diagnosis of chiasmal syndromes.

data.title: Mapping the Dark: Retrochiasmal & Chiasmal Visual Field Defects
data.summary: A comprehensive neuro-ophthalmic guide to localizing lesions posterior to the optic tract, featuring the nuances of congruity, macular sparing, and the differential diagnosis of chiasmal syndromes.

sections.title: Overview of Retrochiasmal Pathways
sections.content: Retrochiasmal lesions involve the optic tract, lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN), optic radiations, and the visual cortex. Unlike pre-chiasmal lesions, these produce contralateral homonymous visual field defects. A fundamental rule in neuro-ophthalmology states: the more posterior the lesion, the more 'congruous' (symmetric) the field defect between both eyes.

rows: Macular sparing (if PCA stroke), Riddoch Phenomenon

sections.title: Optic Tract Syndrome: The Trinity
content: 1. Contralateral Incongruous Homonymous Hemianopia.
2. Wernicke's Hemianopic Pupil: RAPD in the eye with the greater field loss (the eye with the temporal field defect contralateral to the lesion).
3. Bow-tie Atrophy: Primary optic atrophy in the contralateral eye and temporal/nasal pallor ipsilaterally.

content.explanation: PITS: Parietal Inferior, Temporal Superior. PARE: Parietal (decreased) Pursuit, Angular Gyrus (Gerstmann), Reading (Alexia), Extinction (Neglect).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls: Occipital Cortex
content: Congruity: If the defects match perfectly, look at the occipital pole.
Temporal Crescent Sparing: The most peripheral 30 degrees of the nasal field is represented monocularly in the anterior visual cortex.
Riddoch Phenomenon: Perception of motion in a blind hemifield (statokinetic dissociation).
Anton Syndrome: Cortical blindness with denial of vision (anosognosia).

sections.title: The Binasal 'Differential' Mindset
content: Glaucoma: Most common cause; usually respects horizontal, not vertical.
Atherosclerosis: Calcified ICAs compressing the lateral chiasm fibers.
Congenital: Optic Nerve Head Drusen or Tilted Discs.
Neurological: Chiari malformation or hydrocephalus causing 3rd ventricle expansion.

sections.title: Emergency Red Flags
content: Sudden Bitemporal Hemianopia + Headache + Ophthalmoplegia: Suspect Pituitary Apoplexy.
Homonymous Hemianopia + Sudden Neurological Deficit: Rule out CVA (Stroke) immediately.
Progressive Field Loss + Optic Atrophy: Suspect intracranial compressive neoplasm.
Bilateral Blindness with Normal Pupillary Reflexes: Suspect Cortical Blindness (V1 lesion).

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: 1. Automated Static Perimetry (HVF 24-2 or 30-2) for pattern detection.
2. Goldmann Kinetic Perimetry for far peripheral mapping (Temporal Crescent).
3. Pupil Exam: Check for RAPD (Optic tract vs Radiation).
4. DFE/OCT: Check for Bow-tie pallor or RNFL loss.
5. Neuroimaging: MRI Brain & Orbits with/without Gadolinium (Sagittal/Coronal cuts).

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Pseudohomonynous Defects
content: Tilted Discs: Can mimic bitemporal hemianopia but usually crosses the vertical midline.
Functional Visual Loss: Cloverleaf or tubular fields.
Severe Glaucoma: Mimicking hemianopias (check RNFL and Cupping).

sections.title: Surgical & Management Principles
content: Compressive Lesions: Transsphenoidal resection of Pituitary adenomas.
Vascular: Stroke management (antiplatelets, risk factor control).
Rehabilitation: Prisms (Frensel) to shift images into the seeing field.
Training: Saccadic exploration therapy for hemianopia.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearl: Traquair's Junctional Scotoma
sections.content: A junctional scotoma occurs at the junction of the optic nerve and the chiasm. It is characterized by a central scotoma in the ipsilateral eye (optic nerve involvement) and a superior temporal defect in the contralateral eye (compression of the inferior nasal fibers, or 'Willebrand’s knee'). This is a localization 'holy grail' for neuro-ophthalmologists.
